statement: Among people reported to California poison control in 2000 to 2005 with ecstasy intoxication and a recorded blood sodium (188 of 545 cases; Rosenson et al., 2007), low sodium (below 130 mmol/L) was found in 55 of 105 women (52 in 100) and 18 of 83 men (22 in 100), an odds ratio of 3.97 (95% CI 2.08 to 7.59), which is 31 more in 100 women than men among those tested (editors' calculation); sodium was recorded about as often in women (35 in 100) as in men (33 in 100). Within each sex, women with low sodium had higher odds of coma (odds ratio 3.93, 1.20 to 12.90) and of seizure (4.38, 1.74 to 11.00) than women without it, while in men the intervals for coma (0.78, 0.15 to 3.97) and seizure (2.21, 0.69 to 7.07) included 1. These are counts of people who became ill and were reported, not rates in people who take MDMA: sodium was recorded in only 35 in 100 of the cases, and the authors say that spectrum bias, incomplete laboratory data and differences between individuals prevent determining causality. The paper gives neither the amount of fluid drunk nor the amount of MDMA taken, and nothing compares women and men who took or drank the same. The direction is the same, without a test, in the UK series in which 10 of 17 patients and both who died were female (Hartung et al., 2002), in an earlier series of 18 cases with 17 women that the California paper cites and that was not read, and, as described in a narrative review (Campbell and Rosner, 2008; second-hand), in more than 85 in 100 of published symptomatic cases, whose table draws 10 rows from the California series and so is not independent. These series are of young people (mean age 21 in California; 15 to 26 in the UK series), so age cannot be compared. Reasons the authors and the review offer (metabolic and hormonal factors; oestrogen effects on water retention and on the brain's response to low sodium; lower muscle mass and body weight) were not tested.
plain: In California poison-centre records, women with MDMA illness were more likely than men to have a low level of blood sodium: 55 of 105 women (52 in 100) against 18 of 83 men (22 in 100), among those who had their sodium measured. Women with a low level were also more likely to have fits or coma. The reports count people who became ill and were reported, not everyone who took MDMA, and sodium was measured in about a third of them, so this does not show how likely low sodium is in women or men who take MDMA. Nobody has compared women and men who took or drank the same amounts. These were mostly young people (average age 21).
population: People with ecstasy intoxication reported to the California Poison Control System in 2000 to 2005 and given a serum sodium result: 188 of 545 included cases (105 women, 83 men; mean age 21 in both); descriptively, 17 UK patients aged 15 to 26 and published case reports
exposure: Female sex, among people who took ecstasy (MDMA) and became ill; amounts of MDMA and of fluid not recorded
comparator: Men with a recorded sodium; within each sex, people with low sodium against people without
outcome: Serum sodium below 130 mmol/L; coma and seizure among those with and without low sodium
magnitude: California poison control, people with ecstasy intoxication and a recorded sodium (Rosenson): low sodium (below 130 mmol/L) in 55 of 105 women (52.4%) and 18 of 83 men (21.7%), odds ratio 3.97 (95% CI 2.08 to 7.59); of the 73 with low sodium, 55 (75.3%) were women, against 296 of 545 (54.3%) women among all cases. Sodium was recorded in 35.3% of women and 33.3% of men. Within each sex, low sodium against not: coma 3.93 (1.20 to 12.90) in women and 0.78 (0.15 to 3.97) in men; seizure 4.38 (1.74 to 11.00) and 2.21 (0.69 to 7.07); death 1.39 (0.22 to 8.65) and 1.85 (0.16 to 21.70). Editors' calculation: 31 more in 100 women than men had low sodium among those tested (52.4 minus 21.7). UK series (Hartung): 10 of 17 patients and both deaths female. Earlier series cited by the California paper (not read): 17 of 18 women; 2 of 3 in an Israeli series of 32. Narrative review, second-hand: more than 85% of published symptomatic cases female. No rate in women or men who take MDMA can be derived.

evidence.extracted: Of 545 included cases, 296 (54.3%) were women and 249 (45.7%) men. 188 cases (34.5%) had a documented serum sodium, of which 73 (38.8%) were below 130 mmol/L: 55 (75.3%) women and 18 (24.7%) men. Of the 115 with a higher sodium, 50 (43.5%) were women and 65 (56.5%) men. Among those with a sodium, female sex was associated with increased odds of low sodium (odds ratio 4.0, 95% CI 2.1 to 7.6). Among women, those with low sodium had increased odds of coma (odds ratio 3.9, 1.2 to 12.9); among men no increased odds (0.8, 0.15 to 4.0).

evidence.locator: Table 1 and Table 2; Results, paragraph on low sodium among the 188 (p. 167)
evidence.extracted: Table 2, the 188 with a sodium (105 women, 83 men): low sodium 55 (52.4%) of women and 18 (21.7%) of men, odds ratio 3.97 (95% CI 2.08 to 7.59); tachycardia 30 (28.6%) and 42 (50.6%); agitation 30 (28.6%) and 24 (28.2%); hyperthermia 10 (9.5%) and 12 (14.5%); coma 18 (17.1%) and 11 (13.3%); seizure 33 (31.4%) and 18 (21.7%); death 5 (4.8%) and 3 (3.6%). Table 1: sodium documented in 105 (35.3%) of 296 women and 83 (33.3%) of 249 men; mean age 21.2 (SD 6.8) in both. Editors' calculation: among people with a sodium, 31 more in 100 women than men had low sodium (52.4 minus 21.7).

evidence.locator: Table 3; Results, 1st paragraph after Table 3 (p. 168, left column)
evidence.extracted: Odds of each outcome with low sodium against without, within sex (women 55 of 105; men 18 of 83): coma 3.93 (95% CI 1.20 to 12.90) in women and 0.78 (0.15 to 3.97) in men; seizure 4.38 (1.74 to 11.00) and 2.21 (0.69 to 7.07), the text printing 2.11 for the men's seizure odds; death 1.39 (0.22 to 8.65) and 1.85 (0.16 to 21.70). Women with low sodium (55) against those without (50) had about 4 times the univariate odds of coma or seizure; men with low sodium (18) against those without (65) had no increased odds of coma and about double the odds of seizure with wide intervals.

The authors conclude that female sex was associated with increased odds of low sodium, and of coma among women with low sodium, in people with ecstasy intoxication and a documented sodium reported to the poison system in 2000 to 2005, and that spectrum bias, incomplete laboratory data and individual differences prevent determining causality about the sex difference.
evidence.quote: prevent determination of causality about sex differences in the incidence of ecstasy-associated hyponatremia

evidence.locator: Limitations, 1st to 4th paragraphs (starts p. 168, right column; ends p. 169, right column); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 169, right column)
evidence.extracted: The authors say referral bias may produce spectrum bias, with the series representing the more severe outcomes; that no sodium was recorded in 65.5% of cases; that low sodium may be relatively benign and self-correcting in some, with certain individuals predisposed to poor outcomes, which the database could not examine; and that differing body build, kidney function, hydration, coingestions and behaviour limit the ability to say how likely a given population is to develop low sodium. In the Discussion, women were no more or less likely to have a sodium measured, the sex difference may involve metabolic and hormonal factors, the pattern could fit female sex acting as an effect modifier, and multiple confounders preclude any definitive statement on the nature and mechanisms of the observed sex differences. The paper reports no fluid-intake figures and no amount of MDMA (editors' reading of the full text).

evidence.locator: Introduction > Importance, 1st paragraph (p. 165, left column into right column)
evidence.extracted: The authors say the association between female sex and low sodium in ecstasy use had been raised before but no study had formally addressed it; the largest previous published case series had 18 case subjects, 17 of them women (94%); the 28-month UK poisons-service series had 17 patients, 10 women (58.8%), with 2 deaths, both women; a 3-month series of 32 patients at an Israeli hospital had 3 with low sodium, 2 of them women. These earlier series were not read here.

Of the 17 patients, 10 were female and 7 male; both who died were female (15 and 18 years). This is a description of cases reported to a poisons service, with no comparison group and no information on how many women and men took MDMA or were tested.

evidence.locator: Hyponatremia and Ecstasy, 1st paragraph; Table 3 (p. 1855, right column)
evidence.extracted: As described in the review, second-hand: the vast majority of the more than 25 published case reports were in females aged 15 to 30 who took a single dose. Editors' count of Table 3 (32 published cases): 27 labelled F, 1 W and 4 M; 10 rows are taken from the California series (reference 82 in the review) and a 15-year-old female with sodium 125 who died appears to be the first UK death, so the tabulated cases are not independent of the two series.

evidence.locator: Hyponatremia and Ecstasy, the paragraph beginning 'Acutely, the fall in serum sodium' (p. 1857, left column)
evidence.extracted: As described in the review, second-hand: a review of published case reports and series found more than 85% of symptomatic low-sodium patients were female; the California study is said to have documented that women had a significantly higher incidence of symptomatic low sodium, coma and death; the review says the sex difference does not reflect more women taking ecstasy, because other complications are more frequent in men; and it offers oestrogen effects on the brain's sodium pump and on cerebral blood vessels, and lower muscle mass and body weight in women, as possible reasons. Editors' note: the California study is cited in the review as reference 49, which in the review's list is a different 1998 case report (the California paper is reference 82), and its own Table 3 gives death odds ratios of 1.39 (0.22 to 8.65) in women and 1.85 (0.16 to 21.70) in men, both intervals including 1.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-I critical on the card: the people are those who were reported and tested (spectrum and referral bias), sodium was recorded in about a third, the odds ratios are unadjusted for body weight, amount of MDMA, fluid intake or other drugs, and exposure is by history.

inconsistency.note: The UK series and the review's cases point the same way, though they are descriptions without a test.

indirectness.note: Worded for people who became ill and were reported, which is what was studied.

imprecision.note: The main interval (2.08 to 7.59) excludes 1 but is wide; the within-sex odds ratios for coma and seizure have intervals up to 12.90 and 7.07.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the odds ratio (about 4) is large, but the people studied are those reported and tested, and unmeasured differences in body weight, amount taken and fluid drunk could produce or hide it (METHODS 6.3).

grade.reasoning: One poison-centre case series with a comparison inside it starts low (observational). Risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low. Relation: is associated with; the authors themselves say causality cannot be determined, and sex is bound up with body size, amount taken and fluid drunk, none of which was recorded. Status single study: only the California series tests the sex difference; the UK series and the review are consistent but do not test it, and the review overlaps the California series. The answer to who is most at risk cannot be read from this claim: it gives who was found among reported cases with a sodium result, not who is at risk among people who take MDMA, and no age comparison is possible.

verification.flag_note: Rests on one case-series test of sex and descriptive series; stays draft (METHODS 6.3 and 12). The review misreports the California study twice: it cites reference 49 (a different 1998 case report) and says women had significantly higher death, which the study's Table 3 does not show. Within the California paper the text prints 74 low-sodium cases once (73 elsewhere) and 2.11 for an odds ratio the table gives as 2.21; the abstract gives 54.3% women and the Results 54.6%. Table 1 lists 8 women and 5 men among the 13 deaths, while the text and the appendix give 9 and 4 (not used here). The earlier 18-case series (Budisavljevic 2003, Am J Med Sci 326:89-93) was not read; DOI not checked.
